refr.title: Refraction: modelled everywhere, imagined for the plane if need be, checked against the weather
refr.mini: Standard refraction bends light along the curve and makes the Earth look like a larger sphere, R′ = R/(1 − k), k = 0.13: flatter, never flat. Both values are always printed side by side.
refr.text: Refraction is the usual escape, so the site models it everywhere. Light near the ground bends along the curve; seen through standard air, the Earth looks like a sphere of radius R′ = R/(1 − k), with k = 0.13 on average [1], about 1.15 times larger: flatter, never flat. The globe is always computed with and without it, both values side by side. For a photograph, the plane may even be given the refraction it would need to match what is seen, an air chosen in its favour, and the globe too; beside each, the refraction computed from the weather of the day is always written. The question is whether the air each model needs is the air that was there.
excl.title: Setting a value aside: three standard deviations of the others
excl.mini: A value is set aside only if it lies more than three standard deviations from the mean of all the others, that spread measured without it. Never a percentage chosen afterwards.
excl.text: A value is set aside only if it lies more than three standard deviations from the mean of all the other values, the spread being measured without it, in a single pass. For a normal distribution, a value that far out has about 0.3 % chance of being bad luck [1]. Leaving the value out of its own test matters: a wild value inflates the spread it is compared with, and could hide behind it. Never a percentage chosen after seeing the result, and no special treatment for anyone's own measurements.
wmean.title: Combining results: each weighs by its own uncertainty
wmean.mini: Results from different methods are combined as a mean weighted by 1/σ²: a precise method counts more. If they disagree more than their errors allow, the Birge ratio enlarges the error.
wmean.text: Results from different methods are combined as a mean weighted by 1/σ², where σ is each method's uncertainty, its statistical error together with the systematic error measured in its own tab [1]. A precise method counts more. The ratio B = √(χ²/(N − 1)) tests whether the methods agree within their errors; when B is above 1, the error of the mean is multiplied by B rather than ignored [2].
